extracted.intended_audience: architects, art critics, and educated readers interested in church architecture and Christian aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging and designing early Christian churches (plan, ornament, light, furnishings) so that form expresses spiritual character; focused on how architectural elements convey religious meaning and affect worship and preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of the building's spiritual character
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole edifice should be 'expressive at once of the deep sorrow and the sacred courage' of its builders and reflect the Christian state of 'homelessness on earth', making the Most High the habitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin urges fixing on the general character rather than separate details; the emotional and spiritual condition of the builders ought to be manifested in the architecture itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basilica plan and interior proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The church is built on the usual plan of the Basilica: body divided into nave and aisles by two rows of shafts, nave raised above aisles and pierced with small arched windows; at Torcello 'the nave is nearly twice their breadth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interior arrangement and proportions (nave height/breadth, placement and sizing of windows, ranks of pillars) are central to the building's effect; external wall thickness/disposition are less relevant to spiritual expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, variety, and execution of capitals and carving
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals of white marble 'among the best' with every one different in design and showing 'sharp, dark, deep penetrations of the chisel' to achieve calculated effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality and vigorous chisel-work over mere imitation of classical models; variations should be graceful and fanciful rather than indifferent copies (criticizes 'indifferently imitated' Corinthian copies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic ornament (vine, serpent, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamental bands and motifs are often symbolic: the vine is an early symbol of Christ; the wreathed fillet was turned into 'a serpent of three times the length'—typical either of the eternity of his dominion or of Satan subdued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament should integrate theological symbolism so that decorative motifs contribute meaningful religious significance rather than being merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative adaptation of classical motifs (acanthus treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Builders do not slavishly copy classical acanthus: leaves are set with sides outwards, form spirals, are conventionalized into cinquefoiled lobes, rooted in rounded under-stems to give organization and elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative transformation of classical forms—imparting life, elasticity, and growth—is preferable to dead or meaningless imitation; conventionalization may be acceptable if it conveys vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminousness and use of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Torcello's peculiar luminousness: 'frank diffusion of light' allows slight details to be visible even at twilight; sunshine is freely admitted and mosaics avoid artificial shadows and dark colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light should be used to comfort and inspire hope rather than to create darkness or terror; the admission and distribution of light materially affect the spiritual tone of the space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and focus of pictorial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration at Torcello is (or was) simple: mosaics representing 'Christ, the Virgin, and the apostles' at one extremity and 'Christ coming to judgment' at the other, rather than a miscellany of political events, portraits, or grotesques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concentrated, solemn scriptural themes that fix the worshipper's mind on central religious truths; avoid trivial, satirical, or worldly subjects that distract from devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site-specific finish and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'finish and beauty' of the building's portions seem 'actually executed for the place they occupy'; the best pieces appear to have been carved for the island church itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work tailored to the particular site and purpose (rather than transplanted fragments) yields greater unity and appropriateness of effect; craftsmanship should suit its architectural location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reusing carved materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Large surfaces are often covered with sculpture 'for the sake of enrichment only'; architects sometimes cut older carved slabs arbitrarily to fit new uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin views careless refitting not necessarily as savageness but as a sign of 'life in the school of builders' if the new work matches or exceeds the old; reuse is acceptable when it serves architectural effect and is replaced thoughtfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit scale and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulpits 'ought never to be highly decorated'; if the pulpit is very large or splendidly ornamented 'the speaker is apt to look mean or diminutive' and attention may wander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pulpits moderate in scale and free from overwhelming ornament so they do not overwhelm the preacher or tempt the congregation to distraction; excessively magnificent pulpits often lead preachers to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of pulpit ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ornaments admitted 'ought clearly to be of a chaste, grave, and noble kind' and furniture should honor God's word more than provide ease for the preacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulpit decoration should dignify the message rather than glorify the orator; avoid 'ornament of oratory' and prefer restrained, reverent ornament that supports devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-first design for furnishings
rubrics_metrics.description: The pulpit at Torcello is 'slightly oval', allowing free action of the whole person; a carved desk is hollowed so a book 'settles itself there' without slipping; decoration is minimal—six purple marble almonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of pulpits and furnishings should prioritize functional needs of preaching and listening (gesture, book-rest, audibility) while remaining simple and serviceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating and episcopal throne convey dignity through austerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Raised seats and episcopal throne are of marble with 'want of all appliances of comfort' so that arms of the throne are 'not for convenience, but for distinction'—dignity depends on 'utter absence of any expression either of pride or self-indulgence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Austerity and absence of comfort in ceremonial seating can heighten authority and solemnity; comfort that reads as indulgence undermines the symbolic weight of office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural symbolism reinforcing communal identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Christians frequently symbolized the Church as a ship with the bishop as pilot; in island churches this image acquires force—marble ribs and the sweeping ledges can make the structure feel like a temple-ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spatial arrangements and forms that concretely reinforce theological metaphors (e.g., church as ark/ship) to kindle communal memory, obedience, and spiritual courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of ornamentation on preaching and congregational temper
rubrics_metrics.description: The temper in which a congregation listens may be modified by their perception of fitness or unfitness, impressiveness or vulgarity, in the disposition of the speaker's place; ornament can tempt the mind to wander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions (ornament, scale, placement) should consider their psychological impact on worshippers' attentiveness and the preacher's willingness to preach; simplicity fosters receptivity to the 'Divine message.'
